title: Customers and CX
purpose: When customers write in angry, send things back or stop coming back, open Customers and CX to find the cause, fix it and know which customers make money.
fires: the helpdesk export read once a quarter, the retention agency's revenue-based lifetime value deck, and the habit of reading only the angry emails that reach the founder.
not_for: a store under about 100 orders a month, where the founder reads every ticket and knows every repeat buyer by name.

jobs.job: When a month of new buyers came in on paid ads and 90 days later most never came back, tell me why they did not return and what to change first, so I stop paying full price for every sale
jobs.circumstance: Quarterly review, the cohort from 3 months ago is in, 80 percent bought once, ad costs rising, a partner asking why growth feels expensive

progress.functional: know the second order rate by month of first order and the top reasons buyers do not return
progress.emotional: stop feeling that the business is a treadmill that only runs on ad spend
progress.social: show a partner or investor a plan to make each customer worth more, not just a plan to buy more

jobs.hire_today: a retention agency adding more email flows, or Shopify's returning customer percent, or nothing because no one owns the second order
jobs.fire: the blended 'returning customer' number and the habit of blaming email copy for a product or delivery problem

forces.push: every new customer costs full price and most are gone after one order
forces.pull: the reasons first buyers leave, ranked by how many orders they cost
forces.habit: the email agency has always owned repeat buying
forces.anxiety: what if the cause is the product itself and I have to hear it

jobs.little_hire: the first week of each month when a new cohort crosses 90 days

watch.metric: second order rate within 90 days, by month of first order
watch.source: Shopify orders

drives.metric: gross profit per customer at 180 days

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 18 percent of January buyers ordered again within 90 days. After: 23 percent of April buyers did, after fixing the first week of delivery and care messages.
jobs.not_for: a store selling a one-time purchase, like a mattress, where a second order is not the goal

jobs.job: When 'where is my order' messages flood the inbox after a carrier delay, help me get ahead of them with updates before customers ask, so I stop paying agents to answer the same question
jobs.circumstance: Tuesday after a sale weekend, carrier backlog, 300 unread tickets, most about order status, the support lead asking for help

progress.functional: cut order status tickets per 100 orders and know which delays cause them
progress.emotional: stop dreading the inbox every time a carrier slips
progress.social: look to customers like a brand that knows where their parcel is

jobs.hire_today: the support team answering each ticket by hand, or the carrier's generic tracking email
jobs.fire: the carrier tracking page and the copy-paste reply to 'where is my order'

forces.push: each status ticket costs money and tells me a buyer is worried
forces.pull: fewer tickets because customers hear from us first
forces.habit: customers have always just emailed and we reply
forces.anxiety: what if more messages annoy people or promise a date we miss

jobs.little_hire: every week, and the day any carrier reports a delay

watch.metric: order status tickets per 100 orders, 30 day
watch.source: Gorgias tickets joined to Shopify orders

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 11 status tickets per 100 orders. After: 4 per 100 within 30 days of sending 3 updates between order and delivery.
jobs.not_for: a store under about 50 orders a week, where the founder can answer each one in minutes

jobs.job: When returns jump on one product after a new batch or a new page, tell me the reason and the cost, so I fix the product, the page or the size chart before the next 500 orders ship
jobs.circumstance: Monday, the returns pile at the warehouse has doubled for one product, no one knows if it is the batch, the photos or the sizing

progress.functional: know the return rate and top return reason by product, and what it costs in dollars
progress.emotional: stop feeling blindsided by a margin leak I only see at month end
progress.social: give the supplier or the page owner a clear, fair reason to act

jobs.hire_today: the warehouse telling me the pile is big, or the returns app export read once a quarter
jobs.fire: the quarterly returns export and the guess about why

forces.push: returns cost 2 shipping legs, handling and often the product
forces.pull: the cause of a returns spike named in days, not months
forces.habit: returns are seen as a cost of doing business
forces.anxiety: what if I blame the supplier and it was our size chart

jobs.little_hire: weekly, and any week one product's returns rise

watch.metric: return rate by product and return reason, 60 day
watch.source: Shopify returns or the returns app

drives.metric: gross profit after returns, by product, 90 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: the new crew sock runs a 14 percent return rate, mostly 'too small'. After: 6 percent after the size chart and photos changed.
jobs.not_for: a store with so few returns that each one can be read by hand

jobs.job: When a batch problem starts showing up in tickets and reviews, tell me early how many orders it touches, so I stop shipping it and talk to the supplier before a refund wave
jobs.circumstance: Three tickets in 2 days say the seams split on the new batch, the warehouse is still shipping it, a sale starts Friday

progress.functional: know which batch, how many units are out, and how many complaints so far
progress.emotional: stop the sick feeling of finding out from a wave of 1 star reviews
progress.social: go to the supplier with facts, not a hunch

jobs.hire_today: a support agent who happens to notice, or nothing until the reviews arrive
jobs.fire: the habit of reading complaints one at a time without linking them to a batch

forces.push: a bad batch that keeps shipping turns into refunds, returns and reviews for months
forces.pull: an early warning with the count and the batch
forces.habit: support handles tickets, not product quality
forces.anxiety: what if I pull a batch over 3 unhappy customers and it was fine

jobs.little_hire: any week the same complaint appears more than twice

watch.metric: tickets and reviews tagged with the same defect, per batch, 14 day
watch.source: Gorgias tags, reviews app and purchase order records in the brand brain

drives.metric: refunds and returns for defect, 60 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: a bad batch is found after 400 units ship. After: it is held after 60 units, from the third matching ticket.
jobs.not_for: a store that makes each item to order, where there is no batch to hold

jobs.job: When I am about to raise what I pay for a new customer, tell me which customers actually made money after returns, shipping, support and discounts, so I bid only for the ones worth winning
jobs.circumstance: Planning next quarter's ad budget, the agency wants a higher cost per customer target, and I only have revenue per customer to go on

progress.functional: know gross profit per customer at 180 days, by channel, product and first offer
progress.emotional: stop guessing whether growth is making or losing money
progress.social: defend a higher or lower target to the agency with our own numbers

jobs.hire_today: a revenue-based lifetime value from Shopify or an analytics app, or a finance freelancer's one-off spreadsheet
jobs.fire: revenue lifetime value as the number the ad target is set from

forces.push: revenue per customer hides the ones who return half their orders or only buy on deep discount
forces.pull: a profit number per customer that the ad target can be set from
forces.habit: we have always set the target from ROAS
forces.anxiety: what if the profit numbers show our best channel is our worst

jobs.little_hire: before every budget change, and at each quarter end

watch.metric: gross profit per customer at 180 days, by acquisition channel
watch.source: Shopify orders and refunds, product costs in the brand brain, Gorgias tickets

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: the target is $40 per customer for every channel. After: $55 for search buyers worth $90 in profit and $25 for discount buyers worth $30.
jobs.not_for: a store without product costs recorded anywhere, which should fix that first

jobs.job: When the inbox backs up after a big sale and replies take 2 days, help me clear the simple questions fast and keep people on the hard ones, so I do not lose customers to silence
jobs.circumstance: Day 3 after a sale, 600 open tickets, a 2 person team, first reply time at 48 hours

progress.functional: cut first reply time and backlog without hiring for one week
progress.emotional: stop feeling that the team is drowning and it is my fault
progress.social: keep the team's trust that I will not leave them buried

jobs.hire_today: the team working late, a temp from an outsourced support firm, or the founder answering tickets
jobs.fire: the late nights and the founder in the inbox

forces.push: slow replies turn small problems into refunds and bad reviews
forces.pull: simple tickets answered fast so people get time for hard ones
forces.habit: we have always just pushed through peak
forces.anxiety: what if a quick answer is the wrong answer

jobs.little_hire: every peak, and any day backlog passes a set line

watch.metric: median first reply time in hours, 7 day
watch.source: Gorgias

drives.metric: satisfaction score after a ticket, 30 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 30 hour first reply in sale week. After: 6 hours, with order status and address changes answered in minutes.
jobs.not_for: a store with no peaks and a steady, small ticket load

jobs.job: When the payment processor warns that disputes are near the limit, tell me which orders and reasons are driving them and what to change, so I keep my payouts and my account
jobs.circumstance: An email from Shopify Payments or Stripe, dispute rate near 1 percent, payouts at risk, no one tracks disputes separately from refunds

progress.functional: know the dispute rate, the reasons and the orders behind them
progress.emotional: stop fearing the account will be frozen overnight
progress.social: show the processor a real plan if they ask

jobs.hire_today: the founder answering disputes one by one in the payments dashboard, or nothing until the warning
jobs.fire: the one-by-one dispute replies and the habit of treating disputes as bad luck

forces.push: losing the processor means no sales at all
forces.pull: the causes of disputes named, with the fix for each
forces.habit: disputes are handled when they come in
forces.anxiety: what if the cause is fraud we cannot stop

jobs.little_hire: weekly while above half the limit, monthly otherwise

watch.metric: dispute rate, 30 day
watch.source: Shopify Payments or Stripe disputes

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 0.9 percent dispute rate, 70 percent tagged 'not received'. After: 0.4 percent after tracking updates and a clear billing name.
jobs.not_for: a store with almost no card payments, like one paid mostly by bank transfer

jobs.job: When a 1 star review goes up on the best seller and sits at the top of the page, help me answer it well and fix what caused it, so I stop losing buyers who read it first
jobs.circumstance: Saturday morning, a harsh review on the hero product, the page's conversion rate already dipping, the founder angry and tempted to reply in kind

progress.functional: reply within days and fix the cause so the same review does not repeat
progress.emotional: stop taking bad reviews personally and feeling helpless
progress.social: show shoppers reading it that the brand listens and fixes things

jobs.hire_today: the founder replying late at night, or nobody replying
jobs.fire: the late-night reply and the unanswered 1 star reviews

forces.push: new buyers read the worst review first
forces.pull: every bad review answered, with the cause logged
forces.habit: we reply only to the ones that make us angry
forces.anxiety: what if a reply makes it worse in public

jobs.little_hire: every time a 1 or 2 star review lands

watch.metric: share of 1 and 2 star reviews answered within 5 days, 30 day
watch.source: reviews app (Judge.me, Okendo, Yotpo)

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 30 percent of bad reviews get a reply, after 2 weeks. After: all answered within 3 days, and the top cause fixed.
jobs.not_for: a brand with only a handful of reviews a year

jobs.job: When a customer asks to send something back, help me offer an exchange or credit that keeps the sale and refund fast when they want money, so I keep the revenue without an angry ticket
jobs.circumstance: A return request arrives, the customer liked the brand but not the size, the default path is a full refund in 3 weeks

progress.functional: keep more returned value as exchanges or store credit and cut days to refund
progress.emotional: stop feeling that every return is a lost customer
progress.social: look fair and easy to deal with, not like a brand that fights returns

jobs.hire_today: a returns app on default settings, or the support team handling each return by email
jobs.fire: the refund-by-default flow and the slow manual refund

forces.push: a refund loses the sale and a slow one causes angry tickets and disputes
forces.pull: more exchanges and faster refunds without more staff
forces.habit: we set up the returns flow once and never changed it
forces.anxiety: what if pushing exchanges makes customers feel trapped

jobs.little_hire: weekly, and after any policy or returns app change

watch.metric: share of returned value kept as an exchange or store credit, 30 day
watch.source: returns app (Loop, AfterShip Returns) or Shopify returns

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 20 percent of returned value is kept as exchange or credit, refunds take 12 days. After: 38 percent kept and refunds in 4 days.
jobs.not_for: a store that sells one size, one colour items where an exchange makes no sense

jobs.job: When the support lead says 'it has been crazy this week' but cannot say why, tell me what people are contacting us about and which cause is growing, so I fix the cause instead of hiring another agent
jobs.circumstance: Monday team check-in, ticket volume up 40 percent, no tags, each person has a different theory

progress.functional: know the top 5 contact reasons and which one grew
progress.emotional: stop managing by the loudest anecdote
progress.social: give the site, product or ops owner a clear problem to fix

jobs.hire_today: the support lead's memory, or a quarterly read of ticket exports
jobs.fire: the gut sense of 'crazy' and the untagged inbox

forces.push: the same cause costs money every week no one names it
forces.pull: reasons ranked by growth, each with an owner
forces.habit: tickets get answered and closed, never counted
forces.anxiety: what if the tags are wrong and we chase the wrong fix

jobs.little_hire: weekly

watch.metric: share of tickets by top 5 reasons, 30 day
watch.source: Gorgias ticket tags

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 45 percent of tickets have no reason. After: every ticket tagged, and 'discount code did not work' found and fixed in a week.
jobs.not_for: a founder who reads every ticket and already knows why

jobs.job: When customers complain parcels came later than the date we showed, help me show a date we can hit, so I stop creating worry, tickets and refunds with my own promise
jobs.circumstance: Reviews mention 'said 3 days, took 8', a delivery date on the product page set years ago

progress.functional: know how often orders arrive by the promised date, by region and carrier
progress.emotional: stop feeling like the brand breaks promises it did not mean to make
progress.social: look reliable to customers who compare with Amazon

jobs.hire_today: a fixed '3 to 5 days' line on the site, or nothing
jobs.fire: the old fixed delivery line

forces.push: a missed promise causes tickets, refunds and bad reviews
forces.pull: a real date that is right 9 times out of 10
forces.habit: the delivery line was set once and forgotten
forces.anxiety: what if a longer, honest date lowers conversion

jobs.little_hire: monthly, and when changing carrier or warehouse

watch.metric: share of orders delivered by the date shown to the buyer, 30 day
watch.source: Shopify fulfilment events and carrier tracking (AfterShip, ShipStation)

drives.metric: order status tickets per 100 orders, 30 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 71 percent of orders arrive by the shown date. After: 92 percent, with a padded date from real carrier times.
jobs.not_for: a store that delivers locally the same day

jobs.job: When a customer's order went wrong and they are angry, help me fix it in one reply and make it right, so I turn the worst moment into a customer who buys again
jobs.circumstance: A gift arrived late and damaged, the customer is upset, the agent is unsure what they are allowed to offer

progress.functional: resolve failures in one contact and track whether those customers buy again
progress.emotional: stop feeling that a mistake means a lost customer
progress.social: give agents room to act, and look generous when we are at fault

jobs.hire_today: each agent deciding alone, or escalating to the founder
jobs.fire: the escalation to the founder and the one-size apology code

forces.push: a cold, slow fix loses the customer for good
forces.pull: a clear rule for what agents can offer, and proof it pays
forces.habit: agents ask before they offer anything
forces.anxiety: what if generous fixes get abused

jobs.little_hire: any time a failure ticket comes in, reviewed monthly

watch.metric: second order rate of customers with a problem ticket versus those without, 180 day
watch.source: Gorgias tickets joined to Shopify orders

drives.metric: repeat revenue from customers who had a problem, 180 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: customers with a problem reorder at 12 percent, versus 20 percent overall. After: 22 percent, after one-reply fixes.
jobs.not_for: a brand with so few failures that each one gets the founder's personal touch

jobs.job: When a new product has been live for 2 weeks, tell me what buyers are saying about it in tickets, reviews and returns, so I fix problems before the ads scale it
jobs.circumstance: Launch week plus 14 days, ads about to scale, first reviews trickling in, no one has read the tickets for this product

progress.functional: know early complaints, return reasons and rating for the new product
progress.emotional: stop hoping the launch went fine
progress.social: give the ad team a green or red light with reasons

jobs.hire_today: the founder skimming reviews, or nothing
jobs.fire: the hope-and-scale habit

forces.push: scaling ads on a flawed product multiplies the damage
forces.pull: a 2 week read of what buyers say, in one place
forces.habit: we judge a launch by sales alone
forces.anxiety: what if early reviews are too few to trust

jobs.little_hire: 2 weeks and 6 weeks after every launch

watch.metric: return rate, rating and complaint tickets for products launched in the last 60 days
watch.source: Shopify returns, reviews app and Gorgias tags

drives.metric: gross profit per order for new products, 60 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: a launch problem is found at month 3. After: it is found at day 14, before ad spend doubles.
jobs.not_for: a store that launches one product a year and watches it by hand

jobs.job: When Meta reports great ROAS, tell me how much of it came from people who already buy from us, so I stop paying to reach customers who would have come back anyway
jobs.circumstance: Monthly ad review, ROAS looks strong, but many buyers look familiar and new customer counts are flat

progress.functional: know the share of ad purchases from existing customers and their cost
progress.emotional: stop feeling fooled by a number that looks good
progress.social: push back on an agency report with facts

jobs.hire_today: the agency's ROAS report, or nothing
jobs.fire: ROAS as the only proof ads work

forces.push: paying for sales that would have happened anyway
forces.pull: a clear split of new versus existing buyers in ad sales
forces.habit: the agency sets up and reports the ads
forces.anxiety: what if cutting spend on existing customers drops repeat sales

jobs.little_hire: monthly

watch.metric: share of Meta purchases from existing customers, and cost per returning purchase, 30 day
watch.source: Meta Ads Manager and Shopify customer list

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 35 percent of Meta purchases are from existing customers. After: 15 percent, with spend moved to new buyers.
jobs.not_for: a store with a tiny customer list, where almost every ad buyer is new

jobs.job: When the AI support agent refunded an order it should not have, or promised something we do not do, help me set what it may do alone and see every case it got wrong, so I let it work without fearing the next mistake
jobs.circumstance: A customer screenshot shows the bot promised free overnight shipping, and a $300 refund went through with no return

progress.functional: set limits on refunds, credits and promises, and see breaches and reopened tickets
progress.emotional: stop fearing what the bot says while I sleep
progress.social: trust the tool enough to tell the team to rely on it

jobs.hire_today: the helpdesk vendor's default settings, or turning the AI agent off
jobs.fire: the default settings and the all-or-nothing switch

forces.push: one wrong promise costs money and trust
forces.pull: clear limits and a list of every case it got wrong
forces.habit: we switched it on and hoped
forces.anxiety: what if tight limits make it useless

jobs.little_hire: weekly, and after any bad bot reply

watch.metric: AI agent actions above their set limit, and AI-closed tickets reopened, 30 day
watch.source: Gorgias AI agent log

drives.metric: share of tickets resolved without a person, 30 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 9 over-limit refunds a month from the bot. After: 0, and 40 percent of simple tickets still closed without a person.
jobs.not_for: a store that does not use an AI support agent

jobs.job: When a parcel is marked delivered but the customer says it never came, help me decide to reship or refund and claim from the carrier, so I stop paying twice and still keep the customer
jobs.circumstance: A 'delivered, not received' ticket, the third this week in one city, no rule for what to do

progress.functional: know how many such claims, where, and what they cost, with a rule for each
progress.emotional: stop feeling cheated either by carriers or by a few customers
progress.social: treat honest customers well without looking naive

jobs.hire_today: the agent reships every time, or the founder decides case by case
jobs.fire: the case-by-case call and the unclaimed carrier losses

forces.push: paying for the same order twice
forces.pull: a fair rule plus carrier claims filed
forces.habit: we reship and move on
forces.anxiety: what if a stricter rule insults an honest buyer

jobs.little_hire: weekly

watch.metric: 'delivered not received' claims per 1,000 orders, and value recovered from carriers, 30 day
watch.source: Gorgias tags joined to carrier tracking

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 6 claims per 1,000 orders, $0 recovered. After: 4 per 1,000 and 50 percent recovered from carrier claims.
jobs.not_for: a store that ships only with signature on delivery

jobs.job: When new buyers write in during the first week asking how to use, wash or size the product, help me answer it before they ask, so I prevent returns and tickets from people who were just unsure
jobs.circumstance: First week after delivery, how-to tickets repeat, some buyers return instead of asking

progress.functional: cut first-week how-to tickets and returns for 'not as expected'
progress.emotional: stop watching good products come back for simple reasons
progress.social: look like a brand that helps, not one that just ships

jobs.hire_today: support answering each one, or a care card in the box
jobs.fire: the one-off answers and the generic care card

forces.push: unsure buyers return or never reorder
forces.pull: the answer arrives when they need it
forces.habit: we answer when asked
forces.anxiety: what if more emails annoy people

jobs.little_hire: monthly, and after every new product

watch.metric: how-to tickets in the first 14 days after delivery, per 100 orders
watch.source: Gorgias tags joined to Shopify orders

drives.metric: return rate for 'not as expected', 60 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 5 how-to tickets per 100 orders. After: 2 per 100 after a care message 2 days after delivery.
jobs.not_for: a product that needs no set-up, sizing or care

jobs.job: When customers go quiet past their usual reorder time, tell me who is drifting and why before I blast a discount, so I win them back without training everyone to wait for a code
jobs.circumstance: The customer list is shrinking, the email agency proposes a 25 percent off win-back to everyone

progress.functional: know who is past their own reorder window and whether a service problem caused it
progress.emotional: stop feeling that the only lever is a discount
progress.social: look thoughtful to loyal customers, not desperate

jobs.hire_today: a win-back discount flow from the email agency, or nothing
jobs.fire: the same discount to every lapsed customer

forces.push: lapsed customers slip away quietly
forces.pull: the drifting customers, with reasons, before a discount
forces.habit: discounts always get a spike
forces.anxiety: what if they come back only for the code

jobs.little_hire: monthly

watch.metric: share of lapsed customers who order again within 60 days
watch.source: Shopify orders and Klaviyo

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 6 percent of lapsed customers return, all on 25 percent off. After: 9 percent, half with no discount.
jobs.not_for: a product bought once in a lifetime

jobs.job: When I hand support to a new hire or an outside team, help me give them the rules, the tone and what they may approve, so I stop answering tickets myself at night
jobs.circumstance: The founder has run support for 2 years, a new hire starts Monday, everything lives in the founder's head

progress.functional: give a new person the reply rules, limits and voice so they are right on day 1
progress.emotional: stop being the only one who can answer a customer
progress.social: look like a real company to the new hire and the customers

jobs.hire_today: the founder doing it all, or a half-finished Google doc
jobs.fire: the founder answering tickets at night

forces.push: the founder is the ceiling on support
forces.pull: a handover the new person can follow without asking
forces.habit: it is faster to just answer it myself
forces.anxiety: what if they say something off-brand to a good customer

jobs.little_hire: each new hire or outside team, and each time a rule changes

watch.metric: share of tickets answered by someone other than the founder, 30 day
watch.source: Gorgias

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: the founder answers 60 percent of tickets. After: 10 percent, with satisfaction holding at 90 percent.
jobs.not_for: a store that already has a support lead with written rules

jobs.job: When customers send photos of items that arrived broken or crushed, tell me which products and which packing cause it, so I fix the box before paying for more replacements
jobs.circumstance: Damage tickets with photos, same glass item again, replacements going out at full cost

progress.functional: know damage rate by product and packing type, and what it costs
progress.emotional: stop feeling sick every time a photo of a broken item comes in
progress.social: give the warehouse a clear packing change backed by numbers

jobs.hire_today: support sending replacements and the warehouse adding more bubble wrap by feel
jobs.fire: the replace-and-hope habit

forces.push: each damaged order costs the item, the shipping and the customer's trust
forces.pull: the products and packing that break, ranked by cost
forces.habit: damage is blamed on the carrier
forces.anxiety: what if better packing costs more than the damage

jobs.little_hire: monthly, and after any packaging change

watch.metric: damage tickets per 100 orders, by product, 60 day
watch.source: Gorgias tags joined to Shopify orders

drives.metric: replacement and refund cost for damage, 60 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 3 damage tickets per 100 orders on the glass set. After: 0.5 per 100 after a molded insert.
jobs.not_for: a store selling soft goods that cannot break in transit

jobs.job: When the same complaint about the product reaches support every week, help me get it to the person who can change the product or the page, so I stop paying for the same problem
jobs.circumstance: The support team keeps hearing 'the heel slips', product and marketing never see the tickets

progress.functional: turn repeated complaints into a named fix with an owner
progress.emotional: stop the frustration of support shouting into a void
progress.social: show the team their feedback changes things

jobs.hire_today: nothing, because tickets live in the helpdesk and no one else reads them
jobs.fire: the silence between support and product

forces.push: the same fix costs money every week it waits
forces.pull: the top complaints, with counts, in front of the owner
forces.habit: product decisions come from the founder's taste
forces.anxiety: what if a few loud customers do not speak for most

jobs.little_hire: monthly

watch.metric: repeat complaints with no fix assigned, and weeks open
watch.source: Gorgias tags and the brand brain decision log

drives.metric: return rate and rating on the affected products, 90 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: 4 known complaints have run for 6 months. After: each has an owner and 2 are fixed in a quarter.
jobs.not_for: a founder who reads every ticket and owns the product too

jobs.job: When I sit down on Monday, tell me in 2 minutes whether customers are happier or angrier than last week and why, so I know if anything needs me
jobs.circumstance: Monday coffee, 4 tools open, no single read on how customers feel

progress.functional: see the week's changes in tickets, reviews, returns and disputes with a reason
progress.emotional: stop the low hum of worry that something is going wrong unseen
progress.social: walk into the team meeting already knowing

jobs.hire_today: checking the helpdesk, reviews app and returns app one by one, or not looking
jobs.fire: the tab-by-tab check and the habit of not looking

forces.push: problems grow while no one looks
forces.pull: one read that says what moved and why
forces.habit: I check when something feels off
forces.anxiety: what if a summary hides the thing that matters

jobs.little_hire: every Monday

watch.metric: week-on-week change in tickets per 100 orders, bad reviews, return rate and disputes
watch.source: Gorgias, reviews app, Shopify returns and payment disputes

drives.metric: satisfaction score after a ticket, 30 day

jobs.now_after: Example. Now: the founder checks 4 tools when there is time. After: a 2 minute Monday read, and a rise in damaged-item tickets is caught in week 1.
jobs.not_for: a store with one channel and a founder who already lives in the inbox

jobs.job: When I want to thank my best customers without giving away margin, tell me who they are on profit and what they value, so I keep them without teaching them to wait for sales
jobs.circumstance: Year end, a plan to send the top customers a gift, no list of who is truly top by profit

progress.functional: know the top 20 percent by profit and what keeps them buying
progress.emotional: feel good that the thank-you goes to the right people
progress.social: make the best customers feel seen

jobs.hire_today: nothing, or a list of top spenders by revenue
jobs.fire: the revenue-ranked VIP list and the blanket VIP discount

forces.push: the best customers bring much of the profit and can drift quietly
forces.pull: a profit-ranked list with what each values
forces.habit: VIP means biggest spender
forces.anxiety: what if a perk costs more than it keeps

jobs.little_hire: quarterly, and before any VIP program

watch.metric: repeat rate and gross profit of the top 20 percent of customers, 365 day
watch.source: Shopify orders and product costs in the brand brain

drives.metric: gross profit from repeat customers, 365 day
